title: wallabag
content:
wallabag is a web application allowing you to save web pages for later reading. Click, save and read it when you want. It extracts content so that you won't be distracted by pop-ups and cie.

You can install it on your own server, or you can create an account on wallabag.it.

The documentation is available at https://doc.wallabag.org.

You can contribute to it through its dedicated repository, available here: https://github.com/wallabag/doc.

Please read the documentation to see the wallabag requirements.

Then you can install wallabag by executing the following commands:

git clone https://github.com/wallabag/wallabag.git
cd wallabag && make install

Now, configure a virtual host to use your wallabag.

Other methods

Refer to the installation documentation for other installation methods.

This project uses Weblate for translation.

Feel free to help us translating wallabag.

To learn more about developing wallabag, please refer to the contribution guide.

Content extraction relies on Graby, php-readability and ftr-site-config.

Copyright © 2013-current Nicolas Lœuillet nicolas@loeuillet.org

This work is free. You can redistribute it and/or modify it under the terms of the MIT License. See the COPYING.md file for more details.

title: wallabag - Android App
content:
wallabag is a self-hosted read-it-later app.
Unlike other services, wallabag is free and open source.
wallabag for Android is a companion app for wallabag. You need a wallabag account first, which you are going to use in this app.

wallabag is available on the Google Play Store and F-Droid.

wallabag has been made for you to comfortably read and archive your articles. You can download wallabag from wallabag.org and follow the instructions to install it on your own server. Alternatively, you can directly sign up for wallabag.it.

This android application allows you to put a link in your wallabag instance, letting you read your wallabag links offline.

This application was originally created by Jonathan GAULUPEAU and released under the GNU GPLv3. wallabag is a creation from Nicolas Lœuillet released under the MIT License (Expat License).

The android app lets you:

  • Connect to your self-hosted wallabag instance or connect to your wallabag.it account.
  • Supports wallabag 2.0 and higher.
  • Completely ad-free.
  • Increase and decrease the size of the font and also switch between a serif or sans-serif font for a more comfortable reading experience.
  • Switch between numerous themes.
  • Possibility to cache images locally for offline reading.
  • Get articles read via Text-to-Speech feature.
  • Needs no special permissions on Android 6.0+.

On Android versions prior to Android 6.0, wallabag requires the following permissions:

  • Full Network Access.
  • View Network Connections.
  • Run at startup.
  • Read and write access to external storage.

The "Run at startup" permission is only used if Auto-Sync feature is enabled and is not utilised otherwise. The network access permissions are made use of for downloading content. The external storage permission is used to cache article images for viewing offline.

wallabag app is a free and open source project developed by volunteers. Any contributions are welcome. Here are a few ways you can help:

  • Report bugs and make suggestions.
  • Translate the app (you don't have to create an account).
  • Write some code. Please follow the code style used in the project to make a review process faster.

This application is released under GNU GPLv3 (see LICENSE). Some of the used libraries are released under different licenses.

wallabag extracts the article's content (and only its content!) and displays it in a comfortable view.

If you already have an account on Pocket, Readability, Instapaper or Pinboard, you can import your data into wallabag.

If you're a developer and you want to connect your application to wallabag, we offer you an API. Here is the documentation.

You can use wallabag on your computer, thanks to our web application. But you can also take wallabag everywhere. For example, it's possible to save an article on your laptop at work, start to read it on your smartphone in the subway and finish reading it on your ereader in your bed.

wallabag.it is the quality service that you need to host wallabag. For only €11 per year, you'll get a quality hosting, a professional support, automatic upgrades and daily backups.

title: wallabag turns 10
content:
wallabag 🦘turns 10 🎂 ! To celebrate this birthday, we are pleased to announce the release of wallabag 2.6.0.

We developed this release during a year and I want to thank each of the contributors.

I hope you will love the new features and the fixes we made.

Have a look on some new features

wallabag is 10: it's starting to get a little rusty. That's why we made a lot of effort to improve technical stuff, under the hood. Most of this work was done by Yassine: thank you so much! Thanks to him, wallabag can go forward (for the next 10 years?).

Mass action to tag entries, by @Kdecherf

We now have a nice interface on card view (thank you, @Simounet!). A checkbox is available on each card.

And Kevin added the mass tagging feature: what a pleasure to add many tags on several articles!

Enhance the availability of the add a new URL in the web interface, by @Simounet

The "+" icon in the header bar is not so big. When you have a lot of URL to save, it can be painful to click exactly on the icon.

@Simounet increased the clickable area and you can now click on all the header bar.

New setting to show / hide articles thumbnails, by @nicosomb

@Oppen asked us to add a new setting to show or hide articles thumbnails.

This feature is so useful for slow connections or for instances which have few resources.

That's why we developed it for 2.6.0. See below the result when you chose to hide thumbnails.

Update your instance

📈 To update your instance, just run make update. Don't forget to make a backup of your instance (database and files).

🤝 A little reminder that you can support our work on wallabag by sponsoring us on Liberapay or subscribe on wallabag.it. Thanks!

Changelog

You can read the full Changelog on GitHub.

Download wallabag 2.6.0

To download, install/upgrade wallabag, please read our Downloads page.

Need help?

We are on Gitter, ping us!

You can also open a new issue on GitHub.

How can you help us?

By using wallabag, by reporting bugs, by translating wallabag and its documentation, by talking about wallabag to your friends, ...

You can also help us by donating via Liberapay.

title: On the Thermodynamics of Sisyphean Labour
content:
This is a glorified lorem ipsum written to have a nice demo article.

We model the boulder-mountain system as a closed thermodynamic cycle and show, contrary to popular sentiment, that the net work extracted per ascent is exactly zero. It is a calculation, and a short one. We propose that the myth's endurance owes less to its philosophical payload than to the fact that nobody had previously bothered to close the energy balance. We close it here, publish anyway, and decline to discuss the reviewer's third question. A secondary contribution, of interest chiefly to funding bodies, is a lower bound on the number of ascents required before the null result stops being surprising to the person doing the ascending; we find no such bound, and report this finding with confidence.

The core mechanic that makes this analysis possible is boringly simple: the boulder returns to its starting height at the end of every cycle, so $\oint dU = 0$ regardless of the path taken up, down, or sideways into the abyss of narrative interpretation. We don't care about the shape of the slope. After all, any slope with the same start and end elevation gives the same answer.

Introduction

One must imagine Sisyphus happy.

This is a nice sentence and, as far as we can tell, an untested one1. Camus offers the claim without so much as an error bar. We do not begrudge him this: he was working forty years before anyone thought to instrument a boulder. We are not so constrained, and we intend to make full use of the fact.

The question we ask is narrow and answerable: over one complete push-summit-roll cycle, how much useful work does the system yield? The question we do not ask, because it is not ours to ask, is whether Sisyphus is happy about the answer.

Prior work

  • Camus, A. (1942). Le Mythe de Sisyphe. Declines to provide a figure.
  • Homer. Odyssey, Book XI. Describes the punishment; omits the coefficient of friction of the slope.
  • Titus Lucretius Carus. De Rerum Natura. Uses the myth as an analogy for ambition without once mentioning joules.
  • Various gym mirrors. Report anecdotal evidence of work being done. Not peer reviewed.
    • Follow-up mirrors, consulted a year later. Report the same evidence, with less enthusiasm.
    • A single honest mirror, location withheld. Reports no evidence of anything.

To our knowledge, this is the first paper to treat the boulder as a control volume rather than a punishment. This is either a gap in the literature or a mercy, and we decline to speculate on which.

Method

Let $h(t)$ be the boulder's height above the base of the slope and $m$ its mass. Because the cycle is closed the boulder occupies the same height at the start and end of every period $T$, so the net change in gravitational potential energy over one cycle is:

$$ \Delta U = m g \oint_{0}^{T} \frac{dh}{dt}\,dt = mg \big[h(T) - h(0)\big] = 0 $$

This holds for any slope profile, any pace, and any amount of muttering under one's breath, because the integral only cares about the endpoints. Useful work extracted, $W_{\text{out}}$, is bounded above by $\Delta U$ in the idealized (frictionless, tireless) case, which gives us the headline result before we've even opened a laptop:

$$ W_{\text{out}} \le \Delta U = 0 $$

We verified this experimentally as follows:

  1. Select a boulder. Any boulder. Mass is not a free parameter in this experiment; it cancels.
  2. Push the boulder to the summit, recording elapsed time, complaints, and any passing gods.
  3. Release the boulder and allow it to roll to its starting position.
  4. Confirm, by measurement, that the boulder is back where it started.
  5. Repeat for $n = 10^6$ cycles or until funding runs out, whichever comes first.

The state machine governing a single cycle is shown below.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Base
    Base --> Pushing: grasp boulder
    Pushing --> Summit: reach apex (rare)
    Summit --> Rolling: boulder escapes grip
    Rolling --> Base: gravity, unassisted
    Base --> [*]: funding withdrawn

Implementation

The reference implementation is provided below for reproducibility. It has been running unattended since submission.

def push(boulder):
    """Push the boulder one step closer to the summit.

    Args:
        boulder: the boulder currently being pushed. There is
            only ever one boulder; this parameter exists for
            readability, not disambiguation.

    Returns:
        None. The function has no meaningful side effects on
        the boulder's long-run position, only on the pusher.
    """
    boulder.height += 1
    if boulder.height >= SUMMIT:
        boulder.height = 0  # it rolls back; see Section on Method
    return None

if __name__ == "__main__":
    boulder = Boulder(height=0)
    cycles = 0
    while True:
        push(boulder)
        cycles += 1
        assert boulder.height < SUMMIT or boulder.height == 0

Note the assertion on the last line: it is the only test in this codebase, and it has never failed2. We take this as strong evidence for the model, not as an indictment of the coverage.

Results

We ran the loop for $10^6$ ascents. Results are summarized in Table 1.

QuantityValue
Ascents completed1,000,000
Mean height gained per cycle0 m
Net work extracted, $W_{\text{out}}$0 J
Boulders lost0
Boulders regretted1,000,000

The result is stable across all $10^6$ trials to within measurement error, which, since $\Delta = 0$ exactly, is to say it is stable. Boulders regretted exceeds boulders lost by a wide margin. We attribute this to the subject's growing familiarity with the slope rather than any change in the slope itself, and leave the psychometrics to a companion paper we do not intend to write.

Threats to validity

We assume a frictionless boulder and a tireless pusher, neither of which we possess. We consider this an acceptable simplification, in the same spirit as every other paper that assumes a spherical cow, or in this case, a spherical rock.

Conclusion

The system extracts no net work over a closed cycle, a result that will surprise nobody who has ever pushed anything up a hill and watched it come back down. What the myth adds, and what our instrumentation cannot measure, is the account of the walk back down3. One must imagine the reviewer satisfied.

  1. We searched. There is no error bar in the original text, nor in any translation we consulted. ↩︎

  2. It has also never been run against a boulder of negative height, a condition the type system does not rule out. ↩︎

  3. This is, notably, the only part of the cycle during which no work is being demanded of the subject, which our instruments cannot distinguish from happiness. ↩︎
